If you’ve spent any time in the Australian card hobby, you already know what a PSA slab looks like. That red-labelled plastic case has become the universal signal for “this card is legitimate, graded, and ready to trade”. But understanding what the number on the label actually means — and whether your card is worth the cost and wait to get one — is a different question entirely.

This guide covers everything an Australian collector needs: the full PSA grading scale explained in plain English, the four criteria PSA uses to assess every card, a realistic look at Australian submission options and costs, and an honest framework for deciding when grading is actually worth it.

💡 The Key Numbers

PSA 9 and PSA 10 are where the value is. 90% of modern cards submitted to PSA grade at PSA 8 or higher. Only 2–5% achieve PSA 10. Note: PSA raised fees in February 2026 — Economy now starts at USD $32.99 direct (AUD ~$68 via AU dealers). The jump from PSA 9 to PSA 10 is the biggest value cliff in the hobby.

The PSA Grading Scale: 1–10 Explained

PSA uses a 1–10 whole-number scale — no half points, no PSA 9.5. That single gap between 9 and 10 is the most consequential jump in the hobby. Here’s what every grade actually means:

10
GEM MINT
The gold standard
Virtually perfect in every way. Four razor-sharp corners, full original gloss, no staining or marks, pristine edges. Only 2–5% of modern cards achieve this. Worth 4–10× a PSA 9 equivalent.
Centering: 55/45 front • 75/25 back
9
MINT
The sweet spot
Superb condition with only one minor flaw — a very slight wax stain on reverse, minor printing imperfection, or very slightly off-white borders. To the naked eye, appears perfect. The most targeted grade for Australian collectors.
Centering: 60/40 front • 90/10 back
8
NM–MT
Near Mint-Mint
Looks like a PSA 9 at first glance. Upon closer inspection may show slight fraying on one or two corners, a minor printing imperfect or very slight off-centering. Still a strong collector grade.
Centering: 65/35 front • 90/10 back
7
NEAR MINT
NM
Slight surface wear visible on close inspection. Some fraying on corners. Picture focus may be slightly out of register. Most original gloss retained. A solid grade for vintage cards.
Centering: 70/30 front • 90/10 back
6
EX–MT
Excellent-Mint
Visible surface wear or printing defect that doesn’t detract from overall appeal. Very light scratch on close inspection only. Slightly graduated fraying on corners. Some gloss loss.
Centering: 80/20 front • 90/10 back
5
EXCELLENT
EX
Minor rounding of corners. Surface wear and printing defects visible. Minor chipping on edges. Several light scratches visible on close inspection. Some off-whiteness on borders.
Centering: 85/15 front • 90/10 back
4
VG–EX
Very Good-Excellent
Slightly rounded corners. Noticeable but modest surface wear. Light scuffing or scratches. Some original gloss retained. Slightly off-white borders. A light crease may be visible.
Centering: 85/15 front • 90/10 back
3 & below
VG / GOOD / POOR
Collector / vintage grades
Increasing levels of corner rounding, surface wear, yellowing, creases, and gloss loss. Grades 1–3 are primarily relevant for vintage cards (pre-1980) where even low-grade examples hold significant value due to scarcity.
Centering: 90/10 minimum for grades 2–3

The PSA 9–to–10 Cliff: Why It Matters

There is no PSA 9.5. PSA introduced half-grades up to 8.5 in 2008, but deliberately stopped there — keeping the 9-to-10 jump as a binary: your card either reaches perfection or it doesn’t. This creates the most extreme value gap in the hobby:

CardRaw (ungraded)PSA 8PSA 9PSA 10
Wemby 2023 Topps Chrome RC~AUD $30~AUD $80~AUD $170~AUD $600+
LeBron 2003–04 Topps Chrome #111~AUD $800~AUD $3,300~AUD $3,600+~AUD $17,000+

The Four Factors PSA Grades Every Card On

Every card PSA receives is assessed on exactly four criteria. Understanding these is the key to predicting your grade before you submit — and to inspecting cards you’re buying.

⚖️

1. Centering

The most common reason cards don’t reach PSA 10. Measured as a border ratio — PSA 10 requires 55/45 or better on the front. Even 56/44 technically fails. Check centering front, back, and both axes before submitting. Hold the card up to a light source and use a ruler if unsure.

📐

2. Corners

Inspected under magnification. Even microscopic fuzzing or rounding visible under a 10× loupe can drop a card from PSA 10 to PSA 9. Touch-cap damage from handling alone is a common culprit. Always sleeve cards immediately after removing from packs. Never touch corners.

✂️

3. Edges

Look for chipping, fraying, and rough factory cuts. Whitening on dark-bordered cards is a major grade killer — especially common on Topps Chrome and Prizm cards with dark borders. Edge chipping often happens during shipping if cards aren’t packed correctly.

🔍

4. Surface

Scratches, print lines, staining, and gloss loss. Hold the card at a 45° angle under a strong light and tilt it slowly — scratches that are invisible head-on become obvious at an angle. Chrome cards are particularly susceptible to handling scratches from soft sleeves rubbing the surface.

🔬 Pro tip: Self-grade before you submit

Grade your own cards before paying for submission. For each of the four factors, ask: would this pass PSA 10 standards? If any single factor fails, your best-case result is PSA 9. Tools like a 10× jeweller’s loupe (under $15 on eBay) and a bright desk lamp will reveal 90% of what PSA’s graders see.

Is PSA Grading Worth It? The Australian Collector’s Framework

This is the most important question in grading, and most guides avoid answering it honestly. Here’s the truth: for most cards, grading destroys value. Grading fees plus wait time only make sense when the math works in your favour.

The Simple Grading Maths

If result is positive and significant

If result is marginal (under AUD $50 net)

How to Submit Cards for PSA Grading: Step by Step

There are two ways to submit to PSA from Australia: directly through PSA’s own portal, or through an Australian dealer. As of May 2026, direct PSA submissions from Australia are temporarily suspended — Australian dealers are currently the only route. This makes choosing the right local dealer more important than ever.

Option 1: Submit Through an Australian PSA Dealer (Recommended)

  1. Choose your dealer — see the full list below. The Hobby Australia is the only PSA Certified Dealer in the Southern Hemisphere; Card Bot and Mana Market are popular alternatives.
  2. Prepare your cards — place each card in a clear soft sleeve inside a Card Saver I semi-rigid holder. Never use top loaders (too thick) or opaque/matte sleeves. Cards over 130pt thickness can use a top loader.
  3. Complete the submission form — for each card you need: Year, Manufacturer, Set, Player/Character, Card number, Parallel (if applicable), and your estimated grade. Use eBay sold listings to find the declared value (estimated PSA 9 or 10 sale price).
  4. Declare value accurately — this determines your fee tier and your insurance coverage if the card is lost. Be conservative but realistic. PSA can upcharge if the final grade value significantly exceeds your declaration.
  5. Submit and pay — most Australian dealers require payment upfront or on return. Insured return shipping is typically included in the fee.
  6. Track your submission — PSA provides a unique submission number. All Australian dealers provide tracking updates as cards move through the PSA process.
  7. Receive your slabs — Economy tier takes approximately 95 business days (4–5 months) at PSA plus transit. Verify your grades at psacard.com/cert using your certification number.

Option 2: Submit Directly Through PSA

⚠️ Important update — May 2026: PSA has suspended direct international submissions from Australia due to new US tariff changes that apply to the declared value of cards shipped into the US. Submitting directly through PSA’s website is currently not available for Australian collectors. PSA is working on a solution. Until then, Australian dealers are the only submission route — see the full dealer list below.

When direct submissions reopen, the process involves creating a PSA account, paying in USD, and handling all international shipping and insurance yourself. PSA’s current 2026 pricing tiers (when available to Australians directly) are: Value Bulk USD $24.99/card (Collectors Club membership required, 95 business days), Value USD $32.99 (75 days), Value Plus USD $49.99 (45 days), Regular USD $79.99 (25 days), Express and above for higher-value cards. Until direct access resumes, use an Australian dealer — they often achieve comparable all-in pricing once GST, shipping and insurance are factored in.

🇦🇺 Australian market reality

In Australia, PSA dominates. Local Facebook groups, Whatnot and eBay.com.au buyers overwhelmingly prefer PSA slabs for sports cards. For Pokémon, both PSA and CGC have strong demand. BGS is respected but has lower local liquidity — you may need to sell on eBay USA to get full BGS premiums.

💡 The PSA 8 case for value collectors

PSA 8 (NM–MT) gets underrated by collectors chasing PSA 9 and 10. Frequently Asked Questions: PSA Grading in Australia

How much does PSA grading cost in Australia?
Through Australian PSA submission dealers, Economy tier costs from AUD $53 per card (Mana Market, ~95 business days) to AUD $350+ per card for Express (~15 business days). The Hobby Australia, Card Bot, and Slabd are all-inclusive (GST, customs, insurance included). Submitting directly through PSA costs USD $25–$300 per card depending on declared value and tier, plus you handle all international shipping and insurance yourself.
What is the best PSA grade for an Australian collector?
PSA 9 (Mint) is the sweet spot for most Australian collectors — near-perfect condition, strong resale value, and achievable for well-cared-for modern cards. PSA 10 (Gem Mint) commands 4–10× the value of PSA 9 but only 2–5% of modern cards achieve it. For investment purposes, PSA 9 offers the best balance of achievability and value uplift.
How do I submit cards for PSA grading in Australia?
The easiest way is through an Australian PSA submission dealer. The Hobby Australia (Point Cook, VIC) is the only PSA Certified Dealer in the Southern Hemisphere. Card Bot offers Melbourne drop-off and postal submissions nationwide. Mana Market provides published AUD pricing and submits every Tuesday. All handle shipping, insurance and customs on your behalf.
How long does PSA grading take from Australia?
Economy tier takes approximately 95 business days (~4–5 calendar months) at PSA, plus transit time to and from the US (typically 2–3 weeks each way). Total door-to-door on Economy is approximately 5–6 months. Express tiers reduce PSA time to 15–35 business days but cost AUD $180–$350+ per card.
Is PSA grading worth it for Australian collectors?
PSA grading is worth it when: the card is likely to grade PSA 9 or PSA 10, the graded value significantly exceeds raw value plus grading fees, and the card is liquid enough to sell easily in the Australian market. It is generally not worth grading: common modern cards under AUD $100 raw, cards likely to grade PSA 8 or below for most modern sets, or cards where the graded premium doesn’t cover the AUD $53–$110 fee plus 5–6 months of wait time.
What is the difference between PSA and BGS grading?
PSA uses whole-number grades 1–10 and is the gold standard for sports card resale value in Australia. BGS (Beckett) uses half-point grades (including BGS 9.5), provides four sub-grades (centering, corners, edges, surface) on every slab, and has a Black Label 10 Pristine as its top designation. PSA commands higher resale prices for sports cards in the Australian market. BGS is valued by collectors who want detailed subgrade transparency and is popular for vintage basketball.
